newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- NOV 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- NOV 11.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The uncovering of the scandal at the Athens Stock Exchange conceals a more general crisis, with other brokerage firms involved in speculation with the tacit approval of the authorities at the bourse, capital market and depository. There were efforts over the weekend to put the Athens Stock Exchange's house in order. "Whatever is rotten will be cut off," National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou says.

--Crisis on the bourse notwithstanding, the social security funds are seeking a way out of their crisis through the capital market, hoping to increase revenues by capitalising on their property and assets. The government's new spending cutbacks bill will allow funds to invest in shares, with a projected 150 billion drachmas expected to be invested in 1997.

--The government aspires to a finely-tuned budget that will meet the basic targets of the Greek economy's convergence programme to act as a counterpoise to any adverse social and internal ruling party reactions. The 1997 budget will include all the new measures currently being discussed but in a more diluted form than originally thought; measures affecting large social groups are being more carefully handled.
--The development ministry and finance ministry services are preparing to exploit the extensive property and real estate assets of the Greek National Tourism Organisation.
--The Greek telecommunications organisation's (OTE) search for a suitable partner to develop the DCS 1800 mobile phone system is at a critical stage.

--The clean-up operation at the Athens Stock exchange continues over the weekend. "The knife will go down to the bone," National Economy Ministry Secretary-General Apostolos Fotiadis promises, adding that inspectors will be conducting checks of all brokerage firms.

--Bourse authorities worked through the weekend to find ways to cover the 2.6 billion drachma debt left by Delta Securities. Sources say Delta is only the tip of the iceberg and that many other brokerage firms find themselves in the same position of being unable - to a lesser degree - to meet their obligations.

--Greece's electricity company's (DEH) monopoly will be abolished soon, leaving it open to the activity of multinationals. According to reports, the first step to deregulating the market will involve private participation in investment and distribution.
--Turnover at Greece's five casinos has surpassed the 1.7 trillion drachma mark.
--Red tape chokes industry: some state-run firms are in danger of going under due to indecisiveness over their future. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
